Dismissal for misconduct: the disciplinary process step by step

By the Katelago HR team

In twenty years of sitting in these hearings, the reason for the dismissal is rarely the problem. The employee did take the money, or did not come to work, or did swear at the supervisor. Where employers come unstuck is the process they followed to get there.

Namibian law asks two separate questions of every dismissal, and you have to pass both.

Section 33 sets two tests, not one

Section 33(1) of the Labour Act 11 of 2007 says an employer must not dismiss an employee, whether notice is given or not, without a valid and fair reason, and without following a fair procedure.

Read that again and notice the word "and". These are cumulative. A dismissal that is completely justified on the merits is still an unfair dismissal if the process was unfair. Arbitrators find this every week.

Section 48 extends the same test to disciplinary action short of dismissal. Warnings, demotions and suspensions all have to meet it, and action that does not is an unfair labour practice.

The onus sits with you, not the employee

Under section 33(4), the employee only has to establish that a dismissal happened. From that point the dismissal is presumed unfair unless you prove otherwise. You carry the burden of proving both the reason and the process.

This is the single most important thing for a manager to understand. You are not waiting to be proved wrong. You are the one who has to prove you were right, and you do it with the record you kept at the time.

The Act does not tell you how to run a hearing

This surprises people. Section 33 requires "a fair procedure" and then stops. There is no statutory charge sheet, no prescribed notice period for a hearing, no statutory chairperson requirement and no statutory right of appeal.

Section 33 is expressed to be subject to any code of good practice issued under section 137. The only code ever issued in Namibia deals with strikes and lock outs. There is no Namibian code of good practice on discipline or dismissal.

Do not borrow South Africa's code

Most of what comes up in an internet search on this subject is South African, built on Schedule 8 of their Labour Relations Act. That code has no force in Namibia. Applying it will not make your process fair here, and citing it in a Namibian arbitration will not help you.

So where does the procedure come from? Case law

The Labour Court has set out the minimum requirements of a fair disciplinary hearing, and they have been restated consistently. In QKR Namibia Navachab Gold Mine v Dausab, the court repeated the five requirements drawn from earlier judgments in Management Science for Health v Kandungure and Cenored v Ikanga.

  1. Give the employee a concise charge, or charges, in advance of the hearing, so that they can prepare to answer them.
  2. Tell the employee they may be represented by a trade union member or a fellow employee.
  3. Appoint an impartial chairperson.
  4. Give the employee a proper opportunity at the hearing to present their case, and to challenge what the accusers and their witnesses say.
  5. Provide a right of appeal, and tell the employee about it.

Those five are the spine of every defensible Namibian hearing. If you can show all five, you are in a strong position. If one is missing, expect to be asked about it.

Before you charge anyone

Investigate first. Not a conversation in the corridor, a proper look at what happened, who saw it and what the records show.

A simple test: if you cannot write down what the employee is alleged to have done, in one sentence a stranger would understand, you are not ready to charge them.

  1. Establish the facts and secure the evidence while it still exists.
  2. Identify the rule the employee is said to have broken, and satisfy yourself that they knew about it.
  3. Decide whether suspension is genuinely necessary. If it is, it should be on full pay, and it should be short.

Be honest about consistency

If three people did the same thing last year and nothing happened, that history will come up. Consistency of treatment is part of fairness in Namibian law, although an employer is entitled to show valid reasons for treating a case differently. The time to think about that is before you charge, not in the witness box.

The notice of hearing

The employee needs to know what they are answering to, when and where the hearing will be, and what rights they have in the room. Vague charges are the most common defect we see and they are entirely avoidable.

Give reasonable time to prepare. What is reasonable depends on the complexity of the matter, but a notice handed over on the way into the room is not a notice.

The hearing itself

An impartial chairperson who has not been part of the investigation. The employer states its case and calls its witnesses. The employee answers, questions those witnesses and calls their own. The chairperson decides on what was actually presented in the room.

Keep a record. Minutes, or a recording with the employee's knowledge. If it is not written down, it did not happen, and you will be arguing about it a year later from memory.

Two points worth knowing

Your own disciplinary code is a guide to procedure, not something immutable. The Supreme Court has said as much. Sensible departures from your own code, for good reason, will not automatically sink a dismissal.

Holding a second hearing on the same facts after a final warning, with no new information, is not permitted. Decide once, and decide properly.

The sanction, and what follows

Dismissal is not automatic just because misconduct is proved. The chairperson weighs the seriousness, the employee's record, length of service, and whether the relationship can survive.

Then think about severance. Under section 35, severance pay is generally due to an employee with twelve months of continuous service on any dismissal, with an exception for a fair dismissal on grounds of misconduct or poor work performance. Note the word fair. If your misconduct dismissal is later found unfair, that exception falls away and severance becomes payable on top of whatever else is ordered.

How long the employee has

An employee has six months from the date of dismissal to refer an unfair dismissal dispute to the Labour Commissioner, on form LC 21. There is case law on when exactly that six months starts running, because a dispute may only crystallise once internal remedies are exhausted, but do not build a strategy on it.

The practical point for employers is different. Keep your file complete for at least a year. The hearing you handled properly in March is only as good as the record you can produce in November.
